planting.note: Direct sow in earliest spring or in fall for overwintering, into cool, constantly moist, humusy soil; this northern coastal brassica germinates and grows best when temperatures stay well below summer heat and resents drying out between waterings.

directions: Common scurvy-grass is a short-lived rosette-forming brassica that grows wild on damp sea cliffs, salt marshes, and shaded coastal rocks across the cold-temperate and subarctic Northern Hemisphere, and it carries the most literal food-as-medicine history of any plant in this round: ships' crews in the age of sail ate its vitamin-C-rich leaves specifically to stave off scurvy on long voyages. The fleshy, spoon-shaped leaves have a sharp, peppery, slightly salty bite similar to watercress and are best picked young for salads or chopped into sauces; older leaves turn bitter and tough. Give it humus-rich, constantly moist soil and a site with some shelter from the hottest afternoon sun, since it is adapted to cool, often shaded or fog-damp coastal ledges rather than open, baking exposure. It self-sows readily where happy and is usually treated as a cut-and-come-again annual or short-lived biennial, re-sown each season for a reliable spring supply of sharp greens.

planting.note: Root 4-6 inch stem cuttings in spring or late summer in free-draining potting mix, then plant out into fertile, moisture-retentive soil once well rooted; this sport almost never flowers or sets seed, so cuttings are the only reliable way to propagate true plants.

directions: This is a naturally occurring variegated sport of Daubenton's kale, the centuries-old French perennial brassica that never bolts to seed and is propagated entirely from cuttings. Its thick, slightly crinkled leaves are edged in cream to white, making it as much an ornamental foliage plant for a shaded border as a steady, low-effort source of mild, tender kale leaves year-round in frost-free or lightly frosted climates. Like its all-green parent it tolerates a surprising amount of shade for a brassica and can keep producing usable growth with just a few hours of direct sun a day, though some light helps maintain strong variegation and compact growth. Harvest young side leaves regularly to encourage branching, and bring potted specimens under cover where winters drop much below the mid-teens Fahrenheit, since this selection is somewhat less cold-hardy than common kale.

planting.note: Set rooted stem cuttings out once nights stay reliably above 50F into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in a lightly shaded spot; this tropical understory herb is grown almost exclusively from cuttings since it rarely produces viable seed outside its native New Guinea range.

directions: Native to the understory of Papua New Guinea's highland forests, the mushroom plant earns its name from the surprisingly convincing savory, umami, mushroom-like flavor of its fleshy, glossy leaves, which are eaten raw in salads and sandwiches or stirred into soups and stir-fries where the flavor intensifies with cooking. It is a fast-growing, bushy, frost-tender perennial that naturally grows beneath a forest canopy, so it performs best with some shelter from intense midday sun and consistently moist, humus-rich soil; in hot climates deeper afternoon shade keeps leaves lush rather than scorched. Outside frost-free zones it is easily grown as a container herb, brought indoors to a bright window over winter, and propagated freely from stem cuttings rooted in water or moist potting mix. Pinch growing tips regularly to keep plants bushy and productive, and expect small blue flowers in summer if the plant is left unpruned.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or nursery starts in cool, constantly moist, richly organic, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade, ideally beside a shaded spring or stream; like all wasabi, Mazuma collapses quickly if soil temperatures climb much above 70F for long.

directions: Mazuma is one of only a small handful of wasabi cultivars reliably available to growers outside Japan, prized alongside Daruma for its vigor and reasonably forgiving nature by wasabi-farming standards. Its distinctive purple-tinged stems and rhizome mark it out from greener cultivars, and farmers often favor it for fresh paste-making because the finished rhizome delivers a notably strong, clean pungency with a touch of underlying sweetness. Like all wasabi it is an obligate shade and cold-water plant, demanding deep shade, constant moisture, and a long one-and-a-half to two-year growing cycle before the rhizome bulks up to harvestable size, making it a patience-testing but singular crop for a cool, boggy, shaded garden corner. The broad, glossy, heart-shaped leaves are also edible and make an attractive textural groundcover above the slowly swelling rhizome.

planting.note: Sow 4-8 weeks before first fall frost for a winter and early-spring crop, or as soon as soil can be worked in earliest spring; this large-seeded European strain germinates evenly in cold soil that would stall most other salad greens.

directions: Piedmont is a large-seeded continental European heirloom mâche valued for vigorous, slightly larger rosettes and good resistance to the mildew that often plagues this classic cool-season green through damp winters. Its dark green, rounded leaves keep the same mild, nutty flavor typical of mâche but fill out a bit faster and fuller than smaller-seeded strains, making harvest easier on a cut-and-come-again schedule. Mâche is one of the most genuinely shade-tolerant salad crops available, content with the low winter light under deciduous trees or the dappled shade of a cold frame, and it actually prefers the cooler, softer light of a partly shaded bed once days lengthen in spring. Keep soil consistently moist and harvest whole rosettes at the base once they reach full size, since mature plants bolt quickly as the weather warms.

planting.note: Direct sow in late summer through early fall for a fall-to-spring harvest in milder climates, or as early as soil can be worked in spring; large seed size makes Valgros easy to space precisely by hand compared to smaller-seeded mâche strains.

directions: Valgros is a named large-seeded mâche strain grown for its bigger, rounder, dark green leaves and the easier, more uniform germination that bigger seed tends to deliver in cold soil. It forms dense, substantial rosettes with the same mild, nutty character common to all corn salad, standing up well to hard frost and light snow once established. As one of the few salad crops that genuinely thrives in the low light of winter, Valgros is a good choice for the shaded side of a cold frame, under the leafless canopy of deciduous trees, or tucked into a partly shaded bed that would otherwise sit empty through the cool months. Keep the soil evenly moist through germination and harvest whole heads once rosettes fill out, well before any hint of a flowering stalk appears as the days lengthen.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in spring into moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, and set up a trellis, fence, or shrub for the twining vine to climb; named selections like Billington are propagated from tubers or cuttings to keep their improved traits true.

directions: Billington is a named selection of American groundnut maintained and distributed by small perennial-vegetable seed companies for producing larger, more uniform strings of tubers than typical wild-collected stock. Like the straight species it is a nitrogen-fixing, twining legume vine native to moist woodland edges, streambanks, and hedgerows of eastern North America, and it carries the same long food history as a staple tuber crop for many Indigenous nations and early colonial settlers. It thrives in the dappled light of a woodland margin or at the partly shaded edge of a food-forest planting, climbing eagerly over a trellis or companion shrub once established. Tubers take a full growing season or more to bulk up and are best left undisturbed until harvested in fall after the vine dies back, at which point they can be dug, boiled, or roasted like a sweeter, nuttier potato.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in spring into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade to full sun; this line was selected to set a dense string of good-sized tubers in a single season even without a trellis, though yields and vigor still improve with one.

directions: This selection descends from the decades-long American groundnut domestication program run at Louisiana State University under researchers William Blackmon and Berthal Reynolds, who screened thousands of wild and cultivated groundnut plants for larger tuber size, denser tuber set, and the ability to produce a useful harvest in a single growing season rather than the two or more years wild stands typically need. Like all groundnut it is a twining, nitrogen-fixing woodland-edge legume that tolerates considerably more shade than most root vegetables, making it a good match for the dappled light along a fence line, hedgerow, or food-forest understory. Because improved lines like this were bred mainly for untrellised, more compact production, they can be grown as a sprawling ground-covering patch as well as trained up a support. Dig tubers in fall once top growth dies back, and save some uncooked to replant the following spring for next year's patch.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter historical breeding research (Blackmon & Reynolds)

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in spring into moist, sandy to loamy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, with a trellis or shrub nearby for the twining vine to climb; this regional landrace is well suited to the damp, sandy wetland-edge conditions of its native range.

directions: South Jersey hopniss is a regional American groundnut landrace maintained from wild populations native to the damp, sandy soils of the New Jersey Pine Barrens and surrounding coastal plain, kept distinct by small seed-saving growers for its vigor in exactly that kind of acidic, moisture-retentive, part-shaded ground. Like all groundnut it is a twining perennial legume that fixes its own nitrogen while producing strings of starchy, protein-rich tubers, historically an important food source for the Lenape and other Indigenous peoples of the mid-Atlantic region. It is well adapted to the filtered light found along streambanks, pond margins, and the edges of pine-oak woodland, tolerating considerably more shade than most food crops in this database. Allow the vine a full season or more to bulk up its tuber chain before harvesting in fall, and replant a few tubers immediately to keep the patch going the following year.
